title: Event-Driven Systems and Stream Processing
html:
Think about the messages that arrive after you book a ride or place an order. The application may confirm the order first, then send an email, update a delivery estimate, and publish information for analytics. Some of those steps can happen later, although their order and completion rules depend on the product. Charging a customer, for example, may have to finish before the order can truthfully be reported as paid.

Baodium had already taken confirmation email delivery out of checkout in Chapter 4. Chapter 11 also introduced catalog-change events that allowed search to maintain a local copy of product information. The applications no longer waited for those consumers before responding, but they now needed to handle delayed messages, retries, and interrupted processing.

An event records something that has happened, such as an order being confirmed. Publishing that event does not establish that every consumer has completed its own action. Baodium’s notification pipeline shows what durable acceptance, message delivery, and actual completion mean at each stage.

Notification Delivery Architecture

Baodium’s order-confirmation emails are a good place to see both the benefit of events and their cost. Before Chapter 4, Order Service sent the email as part of the checkout request, so a slow email provider made every checkout slow, and a provider error could fail a purchase whose order had already been saved. Today the pipeline has four steps.

  1. Order Service saves the order and an outbox record in a single database transaction.

  2. A relay process reads new outbox records and publishes them to Kafka, a durable message log.

  3. Notification Service reads each event from Kafka and records a task to send an email.

  4. Sender workers submit those tasks to the email provider.

Checkout can now commit the order without waiting for the email provider. Delivery failures are handled after acceptance through the notification pipeline. The outbox and relay still need capacity and monitoring, because a lengthening backlog can delay confirmations to customers.

The transactional outbox from Chapter 3 records the event in the same database transaction as the order. A relay publishes committed outbox records to Kafka later. If the relay or broker becomes unavailable, publication is delayed and the outbox backlog lengthens. The engineers therefore monitored pending outbox records as well as consumer lag, since either stage could delay the confirmation email.

Notification Backlog During Promotion

The outbox committed the notification intent with the order, but it could not improve the email provider’s throughput. Forty minutes into a promotion, customers began reporting that their confirmation emails had not arrived. One engineer suggested doubling the Kafka consumers, expecting Notification Service to be falling behind. The on-call engineer checked consumer lag, the distance between the newest published records and the consumer’s position. It was close to zero. Notification Service was receiving the events promptly.

The delay was in the sender stage. Notification Service was creating email tasks at about 12,000 per minute, but the provider was accepting only about 10,000 per minute from the senders. The difference, 2,000 tasks per minute, was piling up in Notification Service’s database, where the lag graph has no visibility at all. More consumers would only have created tasks faster. They could not have sent a single extra email.

The sender backlog gave the team a different capacity problem from the one they had expected. It also raised a correctness concern. The email provider might accept a submission even if Notification Service lost the response. Those outcomes needed their own records and recovery rules.

An event can also request privileged work. When a refund is accepted for deferred processing, a worker must verify the authorization contract established in Chapter 4 before contacting the payment provider. Kafka delivery proves neither that the person who requested the refund was permitted to do so nor that permission is still valid.

Completion Semantics

When a dashboard says that an event was processed, what has finished? For Notification Service, it was task creation. For each event, the consumer read it from Kafka, wrote a task to the database, and incremented its “processed” counter. At that moment, no email had been sent. The task was waiting for a sender. During the promotion, the counter showed every event processed while hundreds of thousands of emails were still unsent.

The counter was accurate for the stage it measured. The trouble is that each stage finishes a different piece of work, and success at the first stage says nothing about the later ones. Table Table shows what each stage guarantees and what work is left after it.

In this chapter, a notification is submitted once the provider’s acceptance is recorded against its task. Acceptance means the provider took the email, not that it reached an inbox. Delivery reports and bounces measure that separately.

The completion measure must also report tasks that have not finished. A latency chart built only from successful submissions contains only the tasks that were sent, so it understates how long customers have been waiting while a backlog lengthens. The notification team reports the number of overdue unfinished tasks next to completion times. Tasks that are suppressed, canceled, or permanently failed get their own outcomes, because removing a task from the queue is not the same as sending it.

Backlog Growth and Recovery

Once you know what completion means, you can ask how fast a backlog lengthens and how long it takes to clear. During the promotion, tasks arrived at 12,000 per minute and completed at 10,000 per minute, so the backlog increased by 2,000 every minute. After three hours, about 360,000 tasks were waiting. If new orders had stopped completely, the senders could have cleared that backlog in 36 minutes.

New orders do not stop during a promotion, of course. Suppose the team raises sender throughput to 14,000 per minute while tasks are still arriving at 12,000. The first 12,000 completions each minute only match new arrivals, and only the other 2,000 reduce the backlog, so clearing 360,000 tasks takes 180 minutes. Chapter 2 worked through the same arithmetic for a request queue. Written generally, for a backlog BBB, an arrival rate λ\lambdaλ, and a completion rate μ\muμ, the time needed to clear the backlog is Tdrain=Bμ−λ,μ>λ.T_{\mathrm{drain}} = \frac{B}{\mu-\lambda}, \qquad \mu>\lambda.Tdrain​=μ−λB​,μ>λ.

Think of a bathtub with the tap still running. The water level falls when water leaves faster than the tap supplies it. If the completion rate only matches the arrival rate, the backlog never shrinks, and if it exceeds the arrival rate by a small margin, the backlog shrinks slowly. In practice, recovery is slower still, because tasks that fail during recovery are retried and add to the arrivals.

Backlog Size and Backlog Age

Backlog depth tells you how much processing is unfinished. It does not tell you how long customers have been waiting, so the notification team also records the age of its oldest unfinished task. Figure Figure shows how far the two measures can drift apart.

If senders handled tasks strictly in the order they were created, the oldest unfinished task after three hours would be about thirty minutes old, because by then the senders would have completed every task created in the first two and a half hours. Parallel senders, retries, and priorities make that relationship less predictable, so the dashboard reads the age directly from the timestamps of unfinished tasks rather than calculating it.

The dashboard also separates first attempts from retries, because the two indicate different problems. If every task is late, the senders lack capacity. If most tasks finish on time while a small group fails repeatedly, more capacity will not help, and the failing tasks need investigation.

Queues, Logs, and Retention

So far, Kafka has been a pipe between Order Service and Notification Service. To understand what a consumer can recover after a failure, you need to know what Kafka retains, and for how long. Messaging systems use one of two designs, which Figure Figure contrasts.

A queue works like a to-do list shared by a group of workers. Each item goes to one worker, and once that worker confirms it has finished, the item is crossed off and removed. A log works more like a newspaper archive. Every record is added to the end and retained for a set period. Each reader tracks its own place, so many readers can read the same records independently, and any reader can go back and read older ones again.

The difference decides what you can build later. Suppose that, six months after launch, the data team adds an analytics service that reports orders by region. With a log, the new service can read the same order events that Notification Service reads, going back as far as the log retains them, without any change to Order Service. With a queue, those events disappeared as soon as Notification Service handled them, so the new service receives only orders placed after it starts.

Kafka uses the log design. Events are grouped into topics, such as order-events, and each group of consumers tracks its own place in each topic, so Notification Service and the analytics service can read the same events without affecting each other. Traditional brokers such as RabbitMQ, and services such as Amazon SQS, use the queue design, and the rest of this chapter points out where the difference matters.

Retention and Compaction

A log cannot retain everything forever, so Kafka deletes old records according to a retention setting, usually a time limit or a size limit. Deletion happens whether or not every consumer has read the records, so a consumer that is down for longer than the retention period loses the events it missed.

Kafka also offers compaction. Over time, compaction removes older records for a key while retaining that key’s most recent value, subject to tombstone and retention settings. A product-state topic keyed by product identifier can rebuild a local catalog projection from the latest retained values. That projection is current only as far as Catalog has published updates and the consumer has applied them, and historical prices need separate records, because compaction may remove earlier values.

Listing Listing creates one topic of each kind, an order-event topic retained for fourteen days and a product-state topic compacted to the latest record per product. The replication settings come up again when we look at publication.

Retention Sizing

How long should retention be? Longer than the slowest recovery you expect. Suppose a consumer fails on Monday morning, the team needs two days to diagnose and fix it, and the repaired consumer then needs a day to process the events it missed. With two-day retention, Kafka deletes Monday’s events on Wednesday morning, while the consumer is still catching up, and those events are gone from Kafka for good.

The retention period has to cover four intervals, the time to notice the failure, to fix it, to catch up, and to investigate afterward. Once events have been deleted, recovery needs another source, such as an archive or a snapshot of the owning service’s data.

Partitions, Offsets, and Consumer Groups

If each topic were a single log, only one consumer could read it in order, and throughput would be limited to what one process can handle. Kafka avoids that limit by dividing each topic into partitions, independent logs that can be read in parallel. Three terms describe how consumers read them.

Offset.

Every record in a partition has a position number called its offset. Offsets start at zero and increase by one for each new record.

Committed offset.

Each consumer saves the offset it has reached, like a bookmark, so that it can resume from the same place after a restart.

Consumer group.

Consumers that share the work of reading a topic form a group, and the group divides the partitions among its members.

Figure Figure shows a group dividing a topic’s partitions.

Within a group, each partition is read by a single consumer at a time, although one consumer can read several partitions. With twelve partitions and four consumers, each consumer reads three, and with twelve consumers, each reads one. A thirteenth consumer has nothing to read. The partition total is the upper limit on parallelism within a group, and it is the first number to check whenever someone proposes adding consumers.

Message Keys and Ordering

Partitions give you parallelism, but they also change the ordering guarantee. Kafka preserves record order within a partition1, not across partitions. If an order’s OrderShipped event went to partition 3 and its OrderConfirmed event went to partition 7, a consumer could process the shipment before the confirmation.

Producers prevent this by giving each record a key. Records with the same key always go to the same partition, so their relative order is preserved. Order Service uses order_id as the key for order events, so all events for one order are assigned to one partition and are read in the order they were written. Kafka can only preserve the order in which records arrive, however. If the relay publishes an order’s events in the wrong order, Kafka faithfully stores them in the wrong order, as the section on publication shows.

Keys have two further consequences. A single busy key cannot be spread across consumers. If one very large merchant produces a flood of events under one key, they all go to one partition and one consumer, and adding consumers does not speed them up, the same hot-spot problem Chapter 7 met with shards. And changing the number of partitions reshuffles keys. Kafka chooses a partition from a hash of the key and the partition total, so after partitions are added, new events for an order can go to a new partition while its older events wait in the old one. Teams that need more partitions usually create a new topic and migrate consumers to it in a controlled way, so it pays to start with more partitions than you need today.

Out-of-Order Delivery

Even with keys, a consumer can sometimes receive events for one entity out of order, for example when events come from more than one producer, during a replay, or when a producer without idempotence retries a failed send. Each consumer needs a rule for this, and the right rule depends on what the event contains.

Suppose a catalog projection receives product version 12 before version 11. If each event contains the complete product, version 12 is all the consumer needs, so it applies version 12 and discards version 11 when it arrives. If each event describes only a change, such as “price reduced by $5,” applying version 12 without version 11 gives the wrong price, so the consumer must detect the gap and fetch the missing version first. The event contract should say which kind of event it is, because the two kinds need opposite handling.

Event Publication

With partitions and keys in place, you can return to step 2 of the pipeline and look at how the relay transfers events from the outbox into Kafka. Listing Listing shows one published event, and each field has a job.

message_id

identifies this particular event, so a consumer can recognize it if it arrives twice.

event_type and schema_version

tell the consumer how to interpret the payload.

occurred_at

records when the business action happened.

order_version

lets a consumer detect events for the same order that arrive out of order.

This envelope may seem familiar. CloudEvents, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) specification, standardizes much the same set of fields, with names such as id, type, source, and time, and adopting it makes events easier to route and inspect with off-the-shelf tools.

Transactional Outbox Relay

Listing Listing shows the outbox table and the query the relay uses to claim work. The relay repeats four steps.

  1. Claim a batch of the oldest unpublished outbox rows.

  2. Publish each row to Kafka, using the order identifier as the key.

  3. Wait until Kafka confirms it has stored every record.

  4. Mark the batch as published and commit.

Now consider a crash between steps 3 and 4. Kafka has stored the events, but the outbox still shows them as unpublished, because the relay stopped before recording its success. When the relay restarts, it claims the same rows and publishes them again, and Kafka now has two copies of each event in that batch. Marking rows as published before Kafka confirms them would be worse, because a crash could then lose the events altogether. The relay accepts that an uncertain acknowledgment can lead to repeated publication, and every event carries a message_id so that consumers can recognize the repeat without repeating its effect.

The partial index on unpublished rows also gives you the outbox’s most useful health signal. The age of the oldest row with published_at still empty tells you, in seconds, how far publication is behind, whether the relay has crashed, slowed down, or lost contact with the broker.

Relay Sharding

A single relay may not match the rate of a busy outbox, so the notification team runs several. The FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED clause lets each relay claim rows no other relay is working on, without waiting for locks, as you saw for recovery workers in Chapter 3.

Several relays create an ordering problem, though. Relay A might claim an order’s OrderConfirmed event while relay B claims the same order’s OrderShipped event in a separate batch. If relay A is briefly delayed, relay B publishes first, and Kafka stores the shipment ahead of the confirmation. The key sends both events to the same partition, but Kafka stores them in the order it receives them and cannot undo a reordering that happened before publication.

The notification team solves this in three parts. First, the clause on hashtext assigns every order to one of four shards, and each shard has a single active relay, whose previous owner is fenced before any reassignment, using the epoch technique from Chapter 7. Second, the relay publishes each shard’s rows in id order. Third, Order Service guarantees that id order matches business order for each order. That last part needs a closer look. A PostgreSQL sequence hands out numbers when rows are inserted, not when transactions commit, so two concurrent transactions can commit in the opposite order to their identifiers. Order Service avoids this by locking the order’s row before inserting its outbox record, so a later transition for the same order cannot even obtain its outbox identifier until the earlier transaction has committed. As a last line of protection, consumers still check order_version and pause or reconcile when they detect a gap.

The alternative, mentioned in Chapter 3, is a change-data-capture tool such as Debezium, which reads the database’s own change log and publishes outbox rows in commit order. That removes the polling query and the sharding logic, at the cost of another system to deploy, monitor, and upgrade.

Producer Acknowledgments and Durability

Step 3 of the relay loop waits for Kafka to confirm each record, and what that confirmation guarantees depends on the producer settings in Listing Listing.

Kafka stores each partition on several servers, called brokers, so that losing one server does not lose data. A confirmation establishes only as durable as the number of copies that exist when it is sent, and two settings control that.

acks=all

makes Kafka confirm a record only after every in-sync copy has stored it. Together with the topic setting min.insync.replicas=2 from Listing Listing, Kafka refuses writes unless at least two copies can be made. With three copies of each partition, a confirmed event survives the loss of any one broker.

enable.idempotence=true

lets Kafka discard duplicates caused by the relay’s own network retries. Each batch carries a sequence number, and Kafka ignores a batch it has already stored. It also preserves record order when a send is retried, as long as no more than five requests are in flight.

Producer idempotence has a narrow scope, however. It recognizes retries only within one producer session. When the relay crashes and restarts, it begins a new session, and Kafka cannot identify the restarted relay’s records as repeats. Those duplicates are handled by the message_id and the consumer-side deduplication in the next sections.

Delivery Semantics

Now to step 3, where Notification Service reads events. To see what can go wrong there, look at how a consumer tracks its progress.

Every consumer tracks two numbers. Its position is the next record Kafka will hand it, and its committed offset is the bookmark it has saved, the point it resumes from after a restart. By convention, the bookmark points at the next record to read, so after finishing the record at offset 42, the consumer commits 43.

The gap between reading a record and committing the bookmark is where failures cause trouble. Suppose the consumer reads offset 42, creates the email task, and crashes before it commits 43. When it restarts, its bookmark is still 42, so it reads offset 42 again and processes the same event a second time.

At-Most-Once and At-Least-Once

The timing of an offset commit changes what happens if a consumer crashes before finishing a record.

Commit after processing.

When processing finishes durably before the offset is committed, a crash can cause the record to be delivered again. This is at-least-once delivery, provided the broker still retains the record and the consumer resumes correctly.

Commit before processing.

If the offset advances before the business effect is durable, a crash can cause the group to skip that effect after recovery. This is at-most-once processing under that ordering.

For business events, the notification team chose at-least-once, because losing an accepted order’s notification is worse than receiving the same event twice. The second delivery, however, must not cause a second business effect. Every consumer has to be idempotent, meaning that processing the same record twice has the same effect as processing it once, and it needs a clear point at which a record’s work is durably finished, because that is the earliest moment it may commit. For Notification Service, that point is when the email task exists in the database. From then on, the obligation to send the email survives anything that happens to the consumer.

At-most-once has its place too. A stream of frequent sensor readings or page-view analytics may tolerate an occasional lost record more easily than the cost of deduplicating every one. The choice should be made per stream, on purpose.

Consumer Configuration

Many Kafka clients commit the bookmark automatically every few seconds by default. Depending on the client, an automatic commit can advance past a record that is still being processed, especially when the work is handed to other threads, which turns at-least-once delivery into at-most-once. Listing Listing shows the settings Baodium uses instead.

enable.auto.commit=false

The application commits only after the task exists.

auto.offset.reset=earliest

A group with no saved bookmark starts from the oldest retained event rather than the newest. A new group may process some events twice, but it never skips any.

isolation.level=read_committed

The consumer ignores records from producer transactions that were aborted.

max.poll.records, max.poll.interval.ms

These form an agreement with Kafka. The consumer will finish up to 200 records and ask for more within five minutes, and a consumer that misses that deadline is assumed to have failed and loses its partitions.

partition.assignment.strategy, group.instance.id

These reduce the disruption when partitions are reassigned, as the section on rebalancing explains.

Idempotent Consumers

Because Kafka can redeliver a record after a restart, Notification Service creates tasks using the event’s message_id as a deduplication key, with the processed-event marker from Chapter 3 recorded in the same transaction as the task. Listing Listing shows the consumer’s logic.

def process_order_event(record, db, consumer):
    event = decode_and_validate(record.value)

    with db.transaction() as tx:
        first_delivery = tx.claim_event(
            consumer="notification-task-creator",
            message_id=event.message_id,
        )

        if first_delivery:
            tx.create_notification_task(
                event_id=event.message_id,
                order_id=event.order_id,
                notification_type="order_confirmation",
                state="PENDING",
            )

    consumer.commit_next_offset(
        topic=record.topic,
        partition=record.partition,
        offset=record.offset + 1,
    )

The claim has to be a single atomic database operation, not a check and a separate insert, or two copies processed at the same moment would both find nothing and both insert, the check-then-act problem from Chapter 9. Listing Listing shows how to do this in PostgreSQL. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING performs the check and the insert together. When two copies race, one insert succeeds and only that one returns a row, which is how claim_event determines that it is handling the first delivery.

The unique index at the end adds a second safeguard at the business level by allowing at most one confirmation task per order. Even if a producer bug gave the same confirmation two different identifiers, the customer still could not receive two confirmation emails.

Three more rules make the scheme sound. The producer assigns the message_id once, when it writes the outbox row, and every publication retry reuses it. A hash of the payload is not a substitute, because two genuine events can have identical contents. Claims must be retained for as long as an event can be redelivered or replayed, since a repeated event whose claim has been deleted is indistinguishable from a new one. And a consumer that processes several records concurrently may commit only up to the first unfinished record. If offset 42 finishes while offset 41 is still in progress, committing 43 and then crashing skips offset 41 forever.

Idempotent External Deliveries

Idempotent task creation takes care of step 3, but step 4 is harder. Creating a task writes to Baodium’s own database, where a uniqueness constraint can reject a duplicate. Sending an email calls another company’s system, and no constraint in Baodium’s database can reach it. Chapter 3 dealt with the same problem for payments. When the reply to a submission is lost, the sender cannot distinguish a request the provider never received from one it accepted. The remedies are the same here, an idempotency key on each submission and a status lookup to resolve uncertain cases, wherever the provider offers them.

What differs is the cost of getting it wrong. A duplicate payment takes a customer’s money twice. A duplicate email is an annoyance, and some teams decide that a rare duplicate is better than a rare missing email. That can be a reasonable decision, but it should be written into the notification contract, not left to the default behavior of whatever retry library the sender uses. If the provider offers neither an idempotency key nor a status lookup, that trade-off is the only choice you have, and it needs to be made deliberately.

Task States and Leases

Several sender processes share the task table, and any of them can crash halfway through a submission, so each task records its state. Notification Service uses six states.

PENDING

The task is waiting for its first attempt.

SENDING

A sender has claimed the task and is submitting it.

ACCEPTED

The provider has accepted the email.

RETRY_SCHEDULED

The provider rejected the submission temporarily, and the task will be retried later.

UNCERTAIN

A sender stopped during submission, and it is unknown whether the provider received the email.

FAILED

The task has used up its attempts or its time.

Senders claim tasks with a lease, as the recovery workers in Chapter 3 did. Listing Listing shows the claim, including the owner token that stops a sender with an expired lease from overwriting the outcome recorded by another worker.

If a sender crashes, its lease expires and a recovery job finds the task still in SENDING. The recovery job cannot put the task back to PENDING, because the crashed sender may have reached the provider before it stopped, and resending could produce a duplicate. The task becomes UNCERTAIN instead. Because every sender uses the task’s identifier as the provider’s idempotency key, recovery can ask the provider whether that submission arrived and resubmit only if the provider has no record of it.

Exponential Backoff and Jitter

When the provider rejects a submission temporarily, the task becomes RETRY_SCHEDULED, and the sender has to choose when to try again. Chapters 4 and 9 explained why retries need random spacing. Here is the formula the notification team uses, called exponential backoff with full jitter. The maximum delay doubles with each attempt, and the actual delay is a random value between zero and that maximum. delay=random(0, min⁡(cap, base×2attempt)).\text{delay} = \mathrm{random}\bigl(0,\ \min(\mathit{cap},\ \mathit{base} \times 2^{\mathit{attempt}})\bigr).delay=random(0, min(cap, base×2attempt)).

With a base of 10 seconds and a cap of 15 minutes, a task on its fifth attempt waits a random interval of up to 320 seconds. To see why both parts matter, imagine a provider outage that fails ten thousand tasks in the same minute. A fixed five-minute delay would send all ten thousand retries back in the same minute five minutes later, just as the provider recovers. Doubling gives the provider more time with each attempt, and the randomness spreads the retries across that time. After a maximum number of attempts or a maximum age, the task becomes FAILED with a recorded reason, so it shows up as a failed notification instead of disappearing from the backlog.

Exactly-Once Semantics

Kafka supports exactly-once processing for certain transactional consume-transform-produce workflows within Kafka. A transaction that commits Kafka offsets and output records does not atomically commit a PostgreSQL change or an external email-provider request. Notification Service therefore uses a database uniqueness constraint to avoid creating another task when an event is delivered again. Provider idempotency can reduce duplicate submission, but the application still needs delivery-status reconciliation when a provider accepts a request and the response is lost. The guarantee must name the business effect and the system that can verify it.

Decision review

Which stage do you scale?

During the promotion, Notification Service is creating about 12,000 delivery tasks per minute while senders record roughly 10,000 provider acceptances per minute. Kafka consumer lag is low. The backlog of unfinished tasks has been rising for three hours, and the oldest unfinished task is now about thirty minutes old.

Add Kafka consumers, since the event stream is where the work arrives.

Add senders, or raise the provider’s rate allowance.

Defer the promotion’s optional marketing emails until the backlog decreases.

Tasks are created at 12,000 per minute and completed at 10,000, so the backlog increases by 2,000 per minute however many consumers there are.

A adds capacity in front of the backlog. The consumers are already current, so more of them create tasks no faster and send no more email.

B targets the stage where work piles up, but it makes a difference only if sender capacity is the binding limit. If the provider’s rate allowance is the limit, more senders achieve nothing and may trigger rate-limit rejections that resemble a new failure. Find out which limit applies before adding senders.

C reduces the arrival rate. When completion cannot be raised during the incident, reducing arrivals is the other option, and deferring optional marketing emails frees capacity for confirmations without dropping any promised notification. It also raises a question to settle in advance. Should a confirmation that is hours late be sent at all?

Backlog Diagnosis

With completion defined, you can return to the first problem from the incident, finding the stage that is behind. Each stage of the pipeline has its own symptom, and Table Table maps each symptom to the stage it implicates.

Consumer lag is the gap between the newest offset in a partition and the group’s committed offset. It measures progress through the log and nothing beyond it. Low lag shows that the consumer has reached its own finishing point, which for Notification Service is task creation, but it says nothing about the later stages. The sender stage has its own measurements, which are task arrivals, provider acceptances, retries, uncertain tasks, failures, and the age of the oldest unfinished task. Kafka measurements are shown per partition, so that a single overloaded partition does not vanish into an average.

Lag measured in offsets also has a weakness you may recognize from Chapter 7. An offset gap of 10,000 is trivial on a busy topic and serious on a quiet one. Exporters such as Burrow or kafka-lag-exporter turn offset lag into Prometheus metrics, and some estimate lag in time as well, which is usually the more useful number for alerting.

Listing Listing shows the two checks an engineer runs during an incident. For each partition, the Kafka command reports the committed offset (CURRENT-OFFSET), the newest offset (LOG-END-OFFSET), and the gap between them (LAG). During the promotion, lag was in single digits on every partition, while the database query showed hundreds of thousands of pending tasks. Together, the two results put the problem squarely in the sender stage.

Timestamps recorded at each stage, from the order commit to provider acceptance, show where the time went, provided each timestamp has a documented meaning. “Published,” for instance, could mean when the relay sent the event or when Kafka stored it. Clocks on different machines also drift slightly, so an interval calculated from two machines’ timestamps can come out negative. A negative interval points to clock skew or a timestamp bug, and it should be investigated, not rounded to zero.

Consumer and Sender Capacity Scaling

Once task creation had been ruled out, the engineers looked at sender throughput, the provider’s rate limits, and the database work involved in claiming and completing tasks. Extra capacity helps only at the stage where work piles up, and even there it has limits. More consumer processes help when processing is CPU-bound and some partitions are unassigned, but they make a database bottleneck worse by adding concurrent writes, and they cannot speed up a single busy key. More senders help only up to the provider’s rate allowance. Beyond that, they turn a backlog into rejected requests and more retries, which is why the notification team tested higher sender throughput against the provider’s limits before it ever needed it during an incident.

When capacity cannot be raised, the product needs a planned response, in the spirit of the load shedding from Chapter 9. Optional marketing emails can wait, but accepted order confirmations must be sent or marked as failed. Deleting them to shrink the backlog breaks a promise made to customers.

Consumer Rebalancing

Scaling and deployments change the membership of a consumer group, and every change triggers a rebalance, in which Kafka reassigns partitions among the group’s members. A deployment, a crashed consumer, or a consumer that misses its five-minute polling deadline all cause one.

A rebalance resembles a change of workers on a production line, where a station passes to a new worker while the previous worker may still have a half-finished item in hand. Suppose consumer A is processing offset 500 in partition 3. It creates the email task, but before it commits, a rebalance assigns partition 3 to consumer B. Consumer A’s commit is rejected because it no longer owns the partition, and consumer B starts from the last committed offset, which is 500, so the same event is processed twice.

A rebalance is one more source of redelivery, and the protections you already have handle it, namely the claims table, the business constraint, and idempotency keys on calls to the provider. This is a good reason to build idempotency into every consumer from the start, rather than adding it later for particular failure cases.

Some records take longer to process than the polling deadline allows. For those, the consumer hands records to a separate pool of workers and continues polling Kafka in the meantime, so that it is not assumed to have failed. When a partition is taken away, the consumer stops starting new work for it, lets work already in progress finish or cancels it, and commits only offsets whose work is complete.

Two settings from Listing Listing reduce the disruption. The cooperative sticky assignor reassigns only the partitions that need to change, instead of taking every partition from every consumer and redistributing them all, so most consumers continue to work through the change. A fixed group.instance.id lets a consumer that restarts within its session timeout reclaim its own partitions without any rebalance, so a rolling deployment does not reshuffle the whole group.

Consumer Failure Handling

So far the chapter has assumed that every event can eventually be processed. In practice, some cannot, and failures fall into two classes, depending on whether a later attempt can succeed.

Transient failures,

such as a brief database outage, clear up on their own. The consumer retries a limited number of times with increasing delays.

Permanent failures,

such as a malformed event or an unsupported schema version, fail on every attempt. Retrying them wastes capacity and blocks every record after them in the partition.

A permanently failing record has to be preserved, together with the reason it failed, so that someone can repair it. Records that cannot even be decoded need particular care, because they fail before the application’s normal handler runs. A consumer that reads the raw bytes first can save the original payload along with its topic, partition, and offset.

Dead-Letter Topics

Post offices have long maintained a dead-letter office, where mail that cannot be delivered waits until someone works out where it belongs. A dead-letter topic does the same for records that fail permanently. The consumer copies the failed record there and proceeds to the next one, so a single malformed event does not halt an entire partition. Many frameworks support this directly. Kafka Connect, for example, can route certain processing failures to a dead-letter topic through configuration.2

Sending a record to the dead-letter topic only parks it, and the work is still unfinished. The customer still has not received an email. It records that the work is unfinished and hands it to someone who can fix it, so every dead-letter topic needs an owner and its own measurements, such as the number of records waiting and the age of the oldest one. Without an owner, alert, and repair procedure, those records may never be processed again.

Ordering After Failure

Setting a record aside can break ordering. Suppose an OrderConfirmed event fails permanently, the consumer sets it aside, and the next event for the same order is OrderShipped. The consumer now has a shipped order that was never confirmed. It has three options, each with a cost.

  1. Halt the whole partition until the failed record is repaired. Ordering is preserved, but every order in the partition waits.

  2. Pause only that order’s events while processing other orders. That pause must be stored durably, because an in-memory flag is lost on restart.

  3. Use a handler that can rebuild the missing state, for example by asking Order Service for the order’s current status.

Whichever option the team chooses, the repair procedure names an owner and defines how a corrected event goes back into the stream.

Replay and Schema Evolution

Because Kafka retains events, a consumer can reset its bookmark to an earlier offset and process old events again. This is called replay, and whether it is safe depends on what the consumer does with each event.

Replaying events into a catalog projection is safe and often useful. The usual approach is to replay into a fresh destination with a new consumer group, compare it with the current projection, and switch readers once the rebuilt copy has been verified. The Kafka tools make the first step straightforward, as Listing Listing shows.

The group must have no active members when its offsets are reset, and –to-datetime lets you start from a point in time instead of the beginning. Replaying events into Notification Service is another matter, because its effect is sending email. Without the claims table, a replay of 10,000 order events would send 10,000 confirmation emails for orders placed weeks ago. Before any replay, the team decides what the replay is allowed to cause. When customers need a replacement email, for instance because the original used the wrong template, the notification team creates new repair tasks for those customers rather than rewinding a consumer and letting old events run through it again.

Schema Evolution

Replay has a second consequence. A consumer may read events written months ago in an older format, so it must be able to parse every schema version still retained in the topic, not only the current one. A schema registry, as described in Chapter 10, can stop incompatible schemas from being registered, but it cannot decide what a missing field means.

Adding an optional field is safe for new events, but a consumer reading an old event finds the field missing and needs a rule for what that means. If discount_applied is missing, it might mean that no discount was applied, or that the producer did not record discounts when the event was written. The event contract has to define which interpretation applies to each retained schema version.

Changes in meaning are more dangerous than changes in structure. If a field changes from a gross amount to a net amount, its type is unchanged and validation passes, yet every report built on it becomes wrong without any error. A change in meaning needs a new field or a new event version, and consumer tests include sample events from every retained version, because tests against current events cannot catch problems with older ones.

Stateful Event-Time Processing

Every consumer so far handles each event on its own. Some work needs many events together. Baodium’s merchant sales report publishes each merchant’s order total for every five-minute interval. The processor reads order events, adds each order to a running total for its merchant and interval, and publishes the totals. The same pattern shows up in fraud detection that looks at a card’s last hour of transactions, in monitoring that averages sensor readings per minute, and in billing that totals usage per customer per day.

The running total is state, and state brings a failure that independent processing does not have. Suppose the processor adds a $120 order to a merchant’s total and crashes before committing its bookmark. After the restart, it reads the same order again and adds another $120, so the report overstates the merchant’s sales, and no error is ever raised. To prevent this, the processor has to save its state and its bookmark together, in one atomic step.

Stream-processing frameworks such as Kafka Streams and Apache Flink provide that step. They store state locally, back it up continuously, and take periodic checkpoints that capture the state and the bookmark at the same moment. After a crash, they restore both from the same checkpoint, so each event affects the state once. Restoring a large state can take several minutes, during which no new events are processed, so the engineers measured restore time with production-sized data rather than trusting a test with a small one.

Event Time and Watermarks

The report also has to decide which clock assigns an order to an interval. Processing time is when the processor handles the event, and event time is when the order was placed. An order placed at 10:00 but delayed in transit until 10:36 belongs in the 10:00 interval, so the report uses event time.

Event time raises a practical difficulty. The processor has to decide when the 10:00 to 10:05 interval is complete and its total can be published, yet a delayed event for that interval could arrive at any time. A watermark is the processor’s estimate that no more events from before a given time will arrive. Picture a teacher collecting exam papers, who decides how long to wait for latecomers before starting to mark. When the watermark passes the end of an interval, the processor publishes that interval’s total.

Because a watermark is an estimate, some events still arrive after it. The report’s contract defines what happens to these late events. They may revise the earlier total, produce a separate correction, or go to a repair queue. Consumers of the report also need to know which behavior to expect, because a consumer that adds each revised total to the previous one, instead of replacing it, includes the same orders twice.

Consumer Failure and Replay Testing

Each mechanism in this chapter exists to handle an interruption between two durable steps, so the most useful tests create those interruptions on purpose. Baodium’s suite includes these cases.

  • A consumer is stopped after creating a task but before committing its bookmark. The redelivered event must not create a second task.

  • A sender is stopped after the provider accepts an email. The task must become UNCERTAIN and be resolved through the provider’s status lookup.

  • Malformed events, unsupported versions, and events that break business rules pass through the consumer. Each must reach the dead-letter topic with its original payload intact.

  • A rebalance occurs while workers are partway through records.

  • A replay includes old schema versions and events whose claims are near the end of their retention.

  • Recovery is tested while new events are still arriving, not only against a fixed backlog.

Each test is judged by the final outcome rather than by Kafka metrics. Every accepted task must end up sent, durably pending, or recorded as failed, and a drop in consumer lag proves nothing if the work has only relocated to another stage.

Policy Events and Integration Reconciliation

Events carry configuration as well as orders, and the same habits apply. Go back to the deployment-validation service from Chapter 11 and imagine a policy administrator publishing revision 18. The policy database commits the new revision, and three other systems need to hear about it. Jenkins enforces the policy during deployments, a Slack bot posts each change to the team channel, and an audit worker records the history.

The tempting design calls each of them from inside the publication transaction. It works on a good day. On a bad day, Slack is slow, the transaction waits, and no administrator can publish a policy until a chat service recovers. So the publisher does what checkout did in Chapter 3. It writes an outbox record in the same transaction as the revision, and a relay delivers the event afterward.

The event itself should describe a fact and leave each consumer to decide what to do about it. A message called PolicyRevisionPublished, carrying the revision number and a content digest, lets each connector discover that revision 18 exists. Deployment is a separate decision that Jenkins makes under its own checks. Each connector fetches or verifies the revision it needs, updates its own copy, and records which revision it has applied. The policy service still owns the pointer to the active revision, so there is a single place to ask which policy is in force.

That record of applied revisions makes drift visible. A dashboard can show, for each connector, the latest published revision next to the revision it has applied and the time of its last successful check. A connector stuck on revision 17 shows up there even when it has logged no error at all. A reconciliation worker goes one step further. It periodically lists the expected connectors, compares their applied revisions with the published one, and records a repair task for every mismatch, advancing its own checkpoint only after those tasks are saved. That catches the quiet failures, such as a connector that received the event and then crashed before applying it.

Two choices from earlier in the chapter come back here. If each connector only needs its task finished eventually, with bounded retries, a durable work queue is enough. If several consumers need to replay a long history in order, a retained log such as Kafka fits better, with the policy ID or tenant ID as the key so that changes to one policy arrive in order. Ordering applies only within that key, though, so there is no single global sequence across unrelated policies.

Finally, remember the uncertainty rule from Chapter 3. If Jira is unavailable while a worker checks an approval, the worker has no evidence either way. It records INDETERMINATE and schedules a retry under the same operation identity. A timeout is never treated as an approval, and retrying a read must never send a second deployment command.

Scheduled Tasks and Workflow Orchestration

A message queue is a good fit when one worker can finish a task and safely retry it. Some business operations are longer stories. A refund might need a fraud review, a request to the provider, reconciliation, and a final message to the customer, with a human approval and a timer that waits two days somewhere in the middle. If each step travels as an unrelated message, there is no single place to see which steps are done and which compensation is owed when something fails halfway.

The simplest dependable design is a state machine in the database plus scheduled workers, the pattern from Chapter 3. Each operation records its identity, its current state, the states it may enter next, and its retry policy. A scheduled worker picks up eligible operations, claims each one with a lease or a guarded update, records the result, and only then schedules the next stage. For a modest number of workflows, that is often all you need.

When you have many long-running workflows with timers, branches, approvals, and compensations, a workflow engine such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions starts to earn its place. It coordinates the steps and retries for you. It cannot decide the parts that belong to your application, though. You still define the operation identity, the permission checks, and the conditions under which an external action may be repeated, and a workflow history that says “payment sent” proves nothing about the provider until the provider’s own result is verified.

For Baodium’s first notification service, a task table, a managed queue such as Amazon SQS, and the outbox relay were enough. The order commits with its outbox record, the relay delivers the task, and senders update its status. Kafka becomes the better choice once analytics, audit, and other subscribers each need to replay the same business events from their own position. Add that extra machinery when those consumers arrive, and not before.

Summary

The notification backlog hid behind a healthy graph, because the graph measured the wrong stage. That is the first habit this chapter asks you to build. For any asynchronous pipeline, define what finished means at each stage, then measure arrivals, completions, and the age of the oldest unfinished item at every one of them. A backlog becomes easy to locate once you look at where work enters faster than it leaves.

The second habit is designing for interruption. Assume every message can be delivered twice and every process can stop between two steps. The outbox makes publication durable, consumer-side deduplication makes redelivery harmless, idempotency keys and uncertain states make external sends recoverable, and dead-letter topics preserve unprocessable events for repair. Choosing between a queue and a retained log comes down to your consumers, whether they need ordering, and whether they must replay history.

The same accounting of arrivals, capacity, and outcomes carries into a place where every request can succeed while the results get worse. Chapter 13 takes Baodium’s recommendations into that problem.
